transcript:
Header: 2025-02-14 15:00 UTC | Duration: 45m | Recording ID: ff-20250214-00123
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SE), Lina Park (PetaCompute Partnerships), Tom Sanders (PetaCompute Solutions), Evan Li (CloudBridge CTO), Priya Singh (CloudBridge Integration)

Summary: Quick partner intro to explore integration patterns for GPU supply and SI-led deployments.

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maya from Redwood, AE on the partnerships side. We're excited to meet both PetaCompute and CloudBridge — appreciate you making time. Quick round-robin?
[00:18] Lina Park: Hi, Lina here, PetaCompute partnerships. We handle go-to-market with infra partners.
[00:24] Tom Sanders: Tom, solution architect at PetaCompute. I do capacity planning for GPUs and pricing models.
[00:30] Evan Li: Evan, CTO at CloudBridge. We do enterprise integrations and managed deployments for customers.
[00:36] Priya Singh: Priya, lead on integrations at CloudBridge — especially around private deployments and networking.
[00:42] Diego Ramos: Diego, SE at Redwood — I'll be your technical point for benchmarks and integration patterns.

[01:00] Maya Chen: Great. Agenda — quick intros, high-level goals from each partner, discuss integration patterns (hosted API, dedicated pools, private/VPC), perf and pricing constraints, security requirements, and then next steps. Any additions?
[01:15] Evan Li: Sounds good. For CloudBridge, main goal is to understand latency guarantees and what we need to do to make private deployments turnkey for our customers.
[01:25] Tom Sanders: From PetaCompute, we're exploring channel partnerships to allocate GPU inventory to Redwood Dedicated and private offers. We also want to understand scheduling and preemption behavior.

[02:00] Maya Chen: Perfect. Diego, can you give a high-level of how Redwood maps to these patterns?
[02:10] Diego Ramos: Yeah — at a high level we offer three deployment modes: hosted API (easy, multi-tenant), Dedicated (reserved GPU pools for a customer or partner), and Private (VPC/on-prem where the control plane is customer-managed). For partners, we see two common flows: 1) PetaCompute supplies GPU infra to Redwood Dedicated or a co-located cluster that we manage; 2) CloudBridge helps customers run Redwood Private in their VPC or on-prem with our delivery package.
[02:45] Diego Ramos: Important bits: model routing — you can pin models to specific pools, automated fallback to compatible variants, and caching/batching to reduce per-token costs. We also expose telemetry for token-level cost and latency.

[03:20] Tom Sanders: When you say caching and batching, how deterministic is the latency? For enterprise customers low p99 is a must.
[03:32] Diego Ramos: We optimize for p50 and p95 via smart batching and KV cache. p99 can vary with very spiky traffic; that's where Dedicated and reserved capacity help. We also support affinity and isolation for critical routes. There's a tradeoff: aggressive batching helps cost but can add a few tens of ms.

[04:10] Priya Singh: On private side, networking is a big ask. We need to ensure VPC peering or private link options. How do you handle keys and KMS?
[04:22] Maya Chen: We integrate with KMS/HSM for key management. For Redwood Private, customers can use customer-managed keys and we provide audit logs. We'll send the SOC 2 and KMS docs after.
[04:36] Priya Singh: Great. Also curious about model variants — is quantization done server-side or do you expect partners to handle that?
[04:46] Diego Ramos: Runtime supports quantized models and we recommend certain quantization profiles per workload. Model compilation selects kernels based on quantization and hardware. We can onboard both FP16 and int8 variants — your infra just needs to support the runtime requirements.

[05:20] Lina Park: From PetaCompute perspective, our fleet includes A100 and upcoming GH200 nodes; inventory fluctuates month-to-month. We're evaluating whether to offer reserved pools to partners or spot-like allocations.
[05:36] Maya Chen: If you can provide expected capacity windows and pricing, we can map that to Dedicated offers and forecast customer SLAs.

[06:00] Tom Sanders: How does preemption work? If PetaCompute needs to preempt, can Redwood gracefully shift workloads or is there risk of dropped requests?
[06:12] Diego Ramos: We have fallback routing — requests can be routed to compatible cloud regions or model variants. For long-running sessions, we persist KV cache and attempt continuity, but there are edge cases. We'll want to design for graceful degradation with retries and canary policies.

[07:00] Evan Li: For CloudBridge customers, they care about data residency and audit trails. Do you keep logs centrally? Can logs be pushed to customer SIEM?
[07:12] Maya Chen: Audit logs can be exported; we support log forwarders and integrations with SIEM. For Redwood Private, logs remain in the customer's network.

[07:46] Tom Sanders: Pricing — we usually look at effective $/hour per GPU plus network egress. Do you have a pricing model for partner-reserved pools?
[07:58] Maya Chen: We have committed capacity pricing for Dedicated (monthly/annual). For partner programs we can do revenue shares or capacity credits. We'll share a partner pricing sheet after this call.

[08:30] Diego Ramos: Quick caveat on benchmarks — for inference throughput, it depends on model family, sequence length, and batching. We like to run a small benchmark with representative prompts. That helps align on p50/p95 and cost per token.

[09:00] Priya Singh: Ok let's talk about integration patterns. Option A: PetaCompute provides infra and Redwood manages Dedicated endpoint. Option B: CloudBridge deploys Redwood Private into customer VPC using PetaCompute baremetal. Which is easier to operationalize?
[09:18] Diego Ramos: Option A is simplest from our side — Redwood manages runtime and orchestration, you supply capacity. Option B gives customers more control but requires CloudBridge to manage the private control plane and networking — more operations but better for regulated customers.

[10:00] Evan Li: CloudBridge prefers Option B for enterprise customers. We can manage the control plane, but want deployment automation (Terraform, Ansible). Does Redwood provide IaC?
[10:13] Maya Chen: Yes — we provide deployment manifests, Terraform modules, and an on-prem package. For private installs we work with systems integrators for the first few pilots.

[10:45] Lina Park: For Option A, does Redwood need specific host capabilities — like PCI passthrough, MIG, or multitenant GPU?
[10:55] Diego Ramos: We have requirements per model. For example, some large-spin models need MIG disabled and full GPU. For smaller models we can multiplex. We'll share a hardware compatibility matrix.

[11:30] Tom Sanders: About NVlink and model parallelism — if a customer wants very large models, does Redwood support sharded execution across nodes?
[11:40] Diego Ramos: We support model sharding and kernel selection for distributed inference but it's more advanced; most customers prefer smaller shards or specialized instances. We can discuss for any customer use-case during the technical deep-dive.

[12:10] Priya Singh: Security question — SSO and RBAC for multi-tenant dedicated pools: can we integrate with enterprise SAML/OIDC?
[12:20] Maya Chen: Yes, SAML/OIDC for SSO and fine-grained RBAC. For Dedicated and Private we can sync with customer identity providers.

[13:00] Evan Li: On compliance — SOC 2, ISO — what level of attestation do you provide for hosted vs private?
[13:10] Maya Chen: Redwood provides SOC 2 Type II for hosted API. For Private deployments, the responsibility matrix shifts; we provide artifacts and support customers' audits but the control plane being customer-managed changes the scope. We'll send the SOC 2 and PCI/ISO docs for review.

[13:50] Diego Ramos: For benchmarking, a typical workflow: you provide representative prompts, we run scaled-inference runs on target infra, capture latency, throughput, and token costs. We recommend also measuring cold-starts and KV cache hit rates.

[14:30] Tom Sanders: What telemetry do you need from PetaCompute? Host-level metrics, GPU utilization, thermal throttling? We can share Prometheus endpoints.
[14:42] Diego Ramos: Host-level metrics are super helpful. Perf counters, GPU utilization, and network metrics are useful. We can accept Prometheus and offer a connector.

[15:10] Lina Park: Operationally, how do upgrades work? Kernel and runtime updates could affect customers.
[15:20] Diego Ramos: We do staged rollouts with canaries and automatic fallback to older model variants if regressions occur. We also keep per-route version pinning so customers can opt-in to updates.

[16:00] Evan Li: One more — for private installs on-prem, what are the minimum network latency expectations between the control plane and worker nodes?
[16:12] Diego Ramos: Ideally sub-ms within rack, under 1ms intra-datacenter. If network latency is higher then KV cache consistency and some attention ops suffer. We can operate in higher-latency settings but expect degraded p99s.

[17:00] Maya Chen: Let's touch briefly on go-to-market: PetaCompute, would you be open to co-selling or channel credits?
[17:10] Lina Park: Yes, we typically do revenue share and capacity credits for partners. We want to scope a pilot to showcase jointly.

[17:40] Tom Sanders: Pilot idea: Redwood runs a benchmarked customer workload on PetaCompute GH200 nodes via Dedicated for 30 days, CloudBridge supports deployment for a regulated customer. If results are good, expand to more customers.

[18:00] Maya Chen: That sounds actionable. Diego, what's the minimal data we need to run a pilot?
[18:08] Diego Ramos: Representative prompts, expected concurrency, sequence lengths, model family, and target p95/p99 goals. Also infra details: GPU SKU, expected availability windows, and network topology.

[19:00] Priya Singh: Regarding automation, we'll need the Terraform modules and the deployment checklist. Can you share those?
[19:08] Maya Chen: Yes, we'll share Terraform modules and a private deployment runbook.

[19:40] Tom Sanders: A practical constraint — inventory for GH200 may be limited in Q2; we can commit a small reserved pool for pilot if needed. Would Redwood accept dynamic scaling for production?
[19:52] Maya Chen: We support autoscaling and burst policies, but for strict SLAs we'd recommend reserved pools plus burst allowances.

[20:30] Diego Ramos: A note on model variants: if you want lower-cost inference, we can route to quantized int8 variants with slight quality tradeoffs. We can provide eval harnesses so your customers can test regressions.

[21:00] Evan Li: For regulated customers, we also need data deletion guarantees and retention policies.
[21:10] Maya Chen: We support data retention policies and deletion APIs. For Private, data stays in-customer control.

[22:00] Tom Sanders: Any blockers from PetaCompute legal side around shared telemetry or co-sell?
[22:08] Lina Park: We'll need to review a mutual NDA and a partner agreement. I'll get legal engaged once we have the pilot scope.

[23:00] Maya Chen: Sounds good. Diego, can you summarize the technical deliverables?
[23:08] Diego Ramos: Sure — we'll provide: 1) hardware compatibility matrix, 2) benchmark template and script, 3) Terraform modules and deployment runbook, 4) SOC2/KMS docs.

[24:00] Priya Singh: CloudBridge will prepare a network diagram and list of CI/CD constraints. We'll also share the customer onboarding checklist.

[25:00] Tom Sanders: We'll pull together pricing and expected capacity windows and share by next week.

[30:00] [informal discussion about potential customer names and pilots; some crosstalk and brief interruptions omitted] 

[34:00] Maya Chen: Quick note — competitors we see in this space: Nvidia's DGX managed services, some AWS Inferentia-based offerings, and smaller inference cloud players. We think our differentiation is the developer-first API and clear operational controls.

[36:00] Evan Li: If we run the pilot, what's the typical timeline from kickoff to first benchmark?
[36:10] Diego Ramos: Usually 2-3 weeks: infra provisioning, sample prompts ingestion, and 48-72 hours of runs to get stable metrics. For Private installs add another 1-2 weeks for network setup.

[38:00] Priya Singh: For CloudBridge, we also need to confirm customer change window for adding dedicated nodes.

[39:00] Maya Chen: Okay, let's capture explicit next steps. Lina — PetaCompute to send pricing and capacity (due 2025-02-20). Priya — CloudBridge to send network diagram and CI/CD constraints (due 2025-02-19). Diego and I will send infra matrix, benchmark template, Terraform modules, and SOC2/KMS docs by 2025-02-18. We'll schedule the SE-led deep dive for the week of Feb 24.

[40:00] Tom Sanders: Sounds good. One minor question — for fallback routing, is there an API for controlling per-route policies?
[40:10] Diego Ramos: Yes, we expose route configs via API and Console. You can set fallbacks, percent rollouts, and pin models.

[41:30] Evan Li: That addresses our main concerns. I think this is a good kickoff.

[42:00] Maya Chen: Anything else?
[42:10] Tom Sanders: Nothing from me.
[42:13] Lina Park: All good.
[42:20] Priya Singh: No, thanks everyone.

[43:00] Maya Chen: Great — we'll follow up with the deck and docs. Thanks everyone, talk soon.
[44:30] End of recording.
